Tratto dal ponderoso romanzo di Paulo Lins (600 pagine), il film risulta fallimentare sotto tutti i punti di vista. Perché se è vero che le favelas di Rio de Janeiro rappresentano il luogo di un degrado sociale e morale certo profondo e di non facile soluzione, è altrettanto vero che non è con questa operazione che si può sperare di portare un minimo aiuto alla causa. Non risparmiando niente sul piano visivo per quanto attiene a brutalità e violenze e anzi lasciandole uniche, incontrastate protagoniste, il regista vorrebbe far passare l'idea che lui si limita a riprendere la realtà senza intervenire: ma l'eccesso di realismo scavalca il confine della credibilità e fa diventare il racconto più finto della finzione. Dominano allora personaggi come macchiette in mezzo ad un quadro di vita che non restituisce mai la complessità della situazione, essendo insisitito in una sola direzione, quella del crimine e della perdita della vita da adolescenti. Parziale e nichilista, il film accumula solo sconcezze e volgarità, compiacendosi di mostrare bambini sempre più piccoli in giro per le strade pronti ad uccidere, e così impedendo di mettere in piedi qualunque riflessione su quelle situazioni gravi che si vorrebbero (forse, ma non è sicuro) denunciare. Dal punto di vista pastorale, il film è da valutare come inaccettabile, e fortemente negativo.

I honestly don’t understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is. DONT RECOMMEND WATCHING

Can we actually find value in a film that while yes shows the violence people go through when their material needs aren’t met, but doesn’t actually fully call out the cause of the violence? I don’t think so. Especially when the violence towards the men, women, and children is shown as just a symptom and not actually done tactfully. To not have any discussion about the cause of the violence is because of state and police violence, because of class systems, racism, and sexism is irresponsible. Vague pointing at police is not enough. This film says violence begets violence and that right there is the most violent part of this film. These people deserve more. And if all we do is witness the violence can we say we are any better? I don’t think so.

I can’t imagine many of the people who live in The City Of God at the time actually saw this theatrically. And I imagine they would find this distasteful. This is all quite gauche and feels exploitative of real poverty and the trap of poverty. The film deals with race quite strangely as well in a way that made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. Im not really a fan of the style of this either, it’s all very flashy but it kind of makes the characters never feel fully realised. They don’t feel like real people because the movie is more interested in being stylised poverty porn exploitation than a story about people. The idea of gazing at disproportionally black poverty and violence and killing is not interesting to me. Especially when it isnt made for or by the community it is depicting the suffering of. The way death and dead bodies are handled in this film intentionally lacks a level of weight i think to alienate people and upset them. But an image  containing only viscera  divorces the humanity of death and turns it into a spectacle to gaze at. If this came out in an English speaking environment i think people would be more critical of this. Most English speaking audiences don’t really watch films in other languages. I think there is an element of this being an incredibly easy to understand narrative and stylistically familiar enough that more people would give this a shot as a “foreign film”. Which i think lends to a level of exoticism to how some people interact with and engage with the film. Of the few negative reviews i have bothered glancing at a lot of them seem to come from Brazil. There are other crime films i share this criticism with. However there are still several crime films that feel connected enough to the communities depicted in them, to where I feel they are less problematic. The gaze and regard in which this film is held in to me reads as somewhat colonial. The Auteurs and audience domination and extraction of respect, life and humanity in exchange for a narrative that allows people to have their “Harrowing” movie where they get to watch vicariously through an audience surrogate. Where is the framework of media analysis with the response to this film? I genuinely think audiences collectively should scrutinise this film so much more. During my film course at uni there have been several films we have seen where we interrogate how we felt about the film we just watched, we process what it was saying, what it meant, and even at times analysed where the point of view of its conception came from. And sometimes this encompassed the ethics of a film’s conception. And oftentimes this inherently led to the concepts of class dynamics and racism. This is a film that is quite frankly begging for this level of interrogation. And the overwhelming majority of people simply don’t care enough to analyse how the film made them feel the way it did or what it has to say about the context in which the film was made in.

Fernando Meirelles stopped caring about being vocal about crime and poverty once he got the check, and I wouldn't have guessed otherwise. I find this film similar to La Haine in political and contextual terms, but one death in La Haine made me think for days, whereas there is a death every minute in City of God. It's not nearly as moving because the characters have no depth. Every person and the city are reduced to their worst, and it was painful to sit through this viewing. I guess the illusion of fatalism masquerading as social critique is too strong to break.

"City of God" is a technically good film that succeeds where many others fail in its ability to seamlessly connect stories, past and present into one cohesive timeline—though oversimplistically. The cinematography is strange, for better or worse, and the color grading or film (whatever it is) looks good at times, but bad in some scenes. Finally, the acting is mostly great. Unfortunately, "City of God" doesn't want to be anything more than this, instead it's an empty action film with pretty technicalities. What pisses me off the most is that that could have been it—a harmless action movie, it was okay, fun even. Sadly, it's based on a true story about a real town that was experiencing significant gang violence in a country where gang violence was and still is a major problem. The movie so badly wants you to care about the protagonist who's difficult life was largely glossed over in the prologue. I'm supposed to feel a dopamine release as both gangs fight to kill eachother faster, and eventually kill themselves too. This could have been interesting, but it's surface level. Back and forth, betrayal, murder, betrayal, murder. That's all it is—I've summed up the movie. What of the people who live in the city? I don't care about the dude who's family was slaughtered; the movie doesn't want to tell me about them. Instead I should focus on his half hearted revenge arc against the other gang. The movie tries to make you feel the brutality of everything, but you won't. It's all fake. And I just don't believe that the director wanted it to be any other way. He's too cool with it all, and I'm convinced that it's meant to be so—like a fairytale, not a real tragedy, or an on-going problem. An isolated story with an all too happy ending is what we get. Violence continues onto the next generation, but it feels half-hearted, like the director wanted to make a Hollywood blockbuster; small touches of artificial humanity are only put there to make the audience emotional. Characters are empty, blank slates. Poor characterization makes Rocket feel indifferent at times. Mega glorification of all that's bad.

The movie itself is incredibly graphic, but there is a purpose behind it. It shows the violence and hatred that happens when that is all you know, but there is something deep inside us, call it science, human phycology, or a conscience that wonders if there is more to life than fear, rage, and brutality. I did think that was a good message to show that violence doesn’t solve violence. Revenge doesn’t bring satisfaction, peace or closure. Hate cannot solve hate. This messaging however is what it felt like it was trying to say but I was trying to find the moral of this all. Was the purpose of this movie was to tell the loose true story of the characters? The environment and culture of Rio during this time? I felt a bit lost and that messaging I said about hate cannot solving hate was something I had to pull like teeth. Good message? Yes. Hard to find it however. Did I think the of the nudity needed to be in it? No. Since it was a common cinematography and lighting technique to have lots of the violent and graphic acts be done in shadows or heavily implied, I believe the nudity scenes should have followed that same rule of thumb. Imply it. You don’t need the full on images of it unless it tells a story. The consistency of that style of filmmaking didn’t match up with the graphic natures. Another thing about the cinematography was rough. It was shaky in pretty much every single shot and there were SO MANY QUICK shots back to back to back in literal second. It was rough. I had a headache the first few minutes of watching this film and it was the same style for the entire film. It was exhausting and made it difficult to not only follow along, but read the dialogue as well. Not the best choices when it came to film editing.

I've wanted to watch this for years and years, and yet I never did. Maybe there was a reason for that. City of God brims with flair and technique, and there is nary a moment when the image and sound presented aren't well rendered and constructed. But therein lies the issue with this film. It feels too constructed, too amalgamated. The result of a heap of story material set ablaze specifically to hide from sincerity. Is the story true? To a turn, as many of these kinds of stories are. I think where this one falters is that it never seems to stop to consider that it's got one foot in the door of stylized imaginings of a roughly relatable cinematic narrative, and the other in the door of gritty depiction of the lives of the sub-altern. It tends to choose style more than anything else, and in doing so leaves a lot on the table. The flair and flash of its photography, cutting and acting lose quite a bit of their impact by the time you see the 15th or so callous murder--a weightlessness that it feels like the film encourages after a fashion. Simply put: there isn't enough story behind the pomp and circumstance to keep the style engaging. The narrative feels less like a cohesive tableau and more like a series of loosely connected vignettes that are united by violence and excess and not by character presence or investment. Glad I watched it, but I can't say I'm happy with what I watched.

City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. Towards the end of the movie I grew tired of the back and forth between the gang violence, which felt repetitive and held back the pacing. In City of God, though, the city was literally lawless, so the violence didn't have to wait for one generation to die before continuing. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

Assistindo para pesquisa. Acho impressionante o fenômeno de filmes do fim dos anos 90 para início dos anos 2000 nesse ciclo mais mainstream comercial. Claro que hoje tudo é mais padronizado que no passado, mas diria que existe uma forma muito mais explícita na maneira que vários desses filmes se emulavam em suas ideias de linguagem e escolhas narrativas. A ideia do que representava uma encenação de bom gosto tinha uma expressão muito mais clara, até porque existia uma menor quantidade de padrões a ser considerada. E não teria como não entender o grande projeto da retomada neste lugar. Definitivamente existe um primor no que se diz respeito à maneira que o filme se utiliza das personagens. Todos representam em algum lugar uma ideia muito única de si. Mas vejo isso apenas como um embrião que nunca nasce. A virtude se apaga no meio dessa formalização excessivamente programada. Cidade de Deus emula essa montagem ágil dos contemporâneos hollywoodianos. Isso enquanto tenta impor espetacularização em cima de uma banalidade que nunca parece se unir. Enquanto opta por uma narrativa cheia de tropos de outro lugar que não o engloba. Até a metade do filme, essa forma que é uma simbiose meio falha me incomoda menos do que quando decide transformar Leandro Firmino em um adolescente colegial norteamericano com dificuldades em chamar a garota para dançar no baile. Daí em diante a postura dele e do filme assume um caráter falso de infantilização, meio bobo. Eu poderia pensar na voz off didática que impede o filme de acontecer, ou na dramatização meio vazia do filme como um todo. À parte o momento em que Phellipe Haagensen sai de cena, pouco além disso impõe uma intenção dramática. Product of it’s time

O romance sobre o crime organizado geralmente carrega um fundo de crítica social ao se apoiar no "desencanto" da imagem, muito similar ao que concebem como "anti-guerra", por exemplo. O que de fato conecta a denuncia em muitos exemplos, e até em Cidade de Deus . O que nos conduz a essa concepção é a narrativa — cinema é isso —, sobretudo como ela é contada. O primeiro arco de Cidade de Deus se sai muito bem nesse quesito. Montado em causa e efeito, o romance se estabelece em pequenos melodramas, esses que findam em consequências morais acerca do contexto. É notório, portanto, não que o crime seja justificável ou se estabeleça como um ato moral, ele existe, mas o mundo reage. A narrativa, portanto, engloba uma representação da realidade que não é respondida, a reflexão é proveniente da imagem. Ao se deparar com Bené, Zé Pequeno, Cenoura e companhia, a história já é outra, e o mais interessante é que a imagem quase não importa mais. Isso porque a narrativa deixa a diegese de lado e passa a tentar agregar respostas precisas para o que assistimos. Isso é muito claro quando olhamos para esses personagens, sobretudo o quão superficial são essas figuras, que ainda se equiparam a uma simulação de realidade total. A Cidade de Deus nem importa mais, estamos interessados em compreender a tragédia de Zé Pequeno e a ascensão de Buscapé. O retrato do crime organizado se perde em um espetáculo da violência; uma espécie de fascínio.

There is a relentless, sun-drenched velocity to City of God that tricks you into thinking you’re watching a kinetic crime epic, right up until you realize every scene is quietly mourning. What hits hardest on a rewatch isn't just the breathless editing or the electric, samba infused soundtrack it’s how the film treats youth. Kids in the favela aren't given a grace period to just figure things out; they’re forced into adult archetypes before their voices even break. Rocket’s camera lens becomes his only real shield, a way to witness the chaos without letting it consume him entirely, while Lil Zé treats fear as the only currency that matters You could argue it occasionally risks hyper stylizing real world trauma at times, the late 90s post MTV sheen almost feels too sleek for the gravel and sweat it’s documenting. But underneath all that frantic, kinetic energy is a deeply human pulse. It barely lets you catch your breath, not just to thrill you, but because the kids on screen never got to catch theirs either

City of God is a Brazilian crime drama directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund. It is based on real events and portrays life in the Cidade de Deus (City of God) favela in Rio de Janeiro from the 1960s to the early 1980s. The story follows Buscapé (Rocket), a shy and intelligent boy who dreams of becoming a photographer instead of joining the world of crime around him. Through his eyes, the audience witnesses how poverty, violence, and gang rivalries shape the lives of children and teenagers in the favela. At the same time, another boy, Li'l Zé (Zé Pequeno), grows up to become one of the most feared and ruthless gang leaders in the neighbourhood. His desire for power and control leads to brutal conflicts with rival gangs, creating a cycle of violence that affects everyone around him. As Rocket tries to avoid crime and pursue a better future, he documents the reality of life in the favela through his camera. His photographs eventually become a way for the outside world to see the harsh conditions and violence of City of God. City of God is widely regarded as one of the greatest crime films ever made. Its fast-paced storytelling, realistic performances, and striking cinematography create an intense and emotionally powerful experience. The performances feel authentic, with many actors coming from communities similar to those depicted. The nonlinear storytelling keeps the narrative engaging. The cinematography and editing are energetic and memorable. The film realistically portrays how poverty and limited opportunities can trap young people in cycles of violence without glorifying crime. The movie contains strong violence, disturbing scenes, and mature themes, making it suitable only for mature audiences. Some viewers may find its rapid editing and multiple characters challenging to follow at first.

Before you lose your marbles over my rating, allow me to explain. City of God is an incredibly powerful film due to its ability to give you a front row seat into the poverty, violence, sin, and crave for power that this city endures. As someone who is very fortunate to have a safe city to call home, I am struck by the extreme brokenness I’ve witnessed. I am grateful for films that immerse me into to cultures and situations that I am unfamiliar with, and this surely did that. I simply take so many things for granted and can’t imagine the pain these families feel under these conditions. While I’m thankful that I was able to understand this city more, that does not equate to enjoying this movie. As a Christ follower, watching severe sinful acts in various ways play out for the entirety of the film was nearly impossible to bare. Every frame feels wrong to witness. Your heart breaks for how each character really lives their life. Killing, drugs, and meaningless sex are all used as means for joy. Boy am I grateful that this isn’t how we have to live. Rather, there is freedom and joy in the Lord’s law! His command to live holy lives like him points to true life. Because he has a plan and design for each of his beloved children, seeing the slaughtering of kids, raping other men’s wives, gaining power through fear, were all unbearable to see. Since I personally rate movies on how much I like the film, it is hard for me to associate my experience with anything positive. I don’t deny that this is an incredibly important film and that it is a truly special story. I am so glad I watched it. But I don’t think I ever will again.

Ciudad de dios es una hamburguesa del McDonalds para filmbros, lo suficientemente chocante como para ser entretenida y hacerte "pensar" pero no tanto como para realmente dar a ver ideología alguna, incomodar a nadie, ni dejar de ser digerible para un público amplio. Sin más. Siempre me ha parecido una pena que para que un director "extranjero" no solamente no sea ignorado, sino que entre en el canon de mejores películas de la historia, tenga que tener un estilo tan Hollywood. Si miras cualquier lista de mejores películas de la historia, cualquier director asiático, latino, africano... que veas va a ser simplemente un cine espiritualmente americano no solamente estilísticamente hablando, sino en la historia que cuenta. Parece que, en el caso del cine tanto latinoamericano como africano, para que una historia sea apreciada por occidente tiene que ser una pornomiseria diseñada no para dignificar a las víctimas de la violencia sistemática que sacude estos países, sino para entretener a un público extranjero y privilegiado con historias miserables, chocantes y exóticas. Ciudad de dios es el ejemplo más claro que he visto de este fenómeno en mucho tiempo, una película con una trama predecible y satisfactoria en cada giro, en la que el sufrimiento y la escasez de un país entero se reducen a una película de acción telenovelesca con el sentimentalismo más barato que he visto en mi vida. Esto es el máximo exponente del cine colonial, el anti tercer cine ... Glauber Rocha se retuerce en su tumba. Es una película cuya opinión más arriesgada es decir "el crímen es malo no tomeis drogas niños", pero que ni con esas se atreve a analizar ni mínimamente los motivos socioculturales que causan esa criminalidad. Simplemente es una película de acción con buenos y malos, y no entiendo por qué se considera una obra maestra del drama. Pero después de todo, aunque cada momento que pasa más me doy cuenta del choque ideológico que me causa esta película, Ciudad de dios es una tarantinada, y como buena tarantinada que es, es muy entretenida. No es una mala peli, es bastante competente y me ha gustado para pasar el rato. Pero la cantidad de críticos (europeos y americanos, claro) que la ponen entre las mejores de la historia me parece una auténtica locura, y no puedo quitarme de encima la sensación de que este morbo post-colonial está detrás de esas alabanzas, como tantas otras veces.

To be perfectly honest I'm currently unsure how to write this review because I'm still utterly baffled as to how City of God has been elevated to, pardon the joke, a god-like status. I can respect Meirelles for the brutal reality he's shown on screen and I found a few of the performances decent, but for the most part I found the film completely unwatchable for both it's disjointed narrative and obnoxious visuals. To begin I hated the way City of God handled it's multiple story lines. The film opened with a half an hour segment that features the protagonist's brother, a segment of the film that doesn't actually affect the rest of the story besides setting up the Lil' Dice character. Seeing as later in the film Lil' Dice gets reintroduced to us as Li'l Zé, with a whole little montage of Lil' Dice's experience in the hood, that rendered the opening 30 minutes completely pointless from a narrative point of view. The two biggest things I didn't like about the multiple narratives would be the constant narration from Rocket and how abruptly the stories would intertwine. First off, character narration is my biggest gripe about any movie, and it's got all the traits I hate about it in this film. Characters are introduced to us via an impersonal freeze-frame voice over monologue, rather than giving us a natural introduction through dialogue. Narration is used to mask progression in time, rather than simply showing us a montage of events. The narration is delivered in an extremely dry and emotionless manor, which becomes very annoying to listen to. Exposition is frequently delivered to us via voice over, like the character introductions, rather than just giving it to us subtly through dialogue. I feel like I have to write this in every review that features narration. A character's voice over just feels like a cheap way of feeding the audience information without utilizing the language of film. On top of that voice over is a very formal and impersonal way of presenting a story, making us feel disconnected from most characters besides the person consistently talking in our ear. If you're writing a script and it doesn't make sense without having someone literally explain the story to the audience, you have to re-write your script, which is something that should have been done with City of God . The other big thing I didn't like about the narrative was the intertwined stories. Take what was titled the "Knockout Ned story" for instance. In the middle of Ned's story, there were multiple scenes of Rocket working at a newspaper and taking photos in the hood. I don't really understand why the film went through all the effort of even giving us a subtitle for every chapter, when they're just going to freely inter-cut different stories along with it. I actually liked the ambition with the film and I really enjoyed all the character based stories, but I don't feel such a diverse story works if they try to simultaneously split up all the narratives while also editing them together. It made for a film that was inherently difficult to follow because they're attempting to build a kind of formality with the structure while also being very loose about when they told each story. Probably my least favourite thing about the film would be the visuals. I just felt everything was thrown at the camera without any attempts at properly constructing a scene. The camera darting and shaking so frequently that when there was a rare still moment I felt I could finally enjoy watching the film again. I'm not exaggerating when I say I found the film extremely challenging just to watch, which is made even more difficult with the straight-up ugly orange filter everything has. If the visuals were made intentionally unbearable I would understand, maybe the director was attempting to create a film that visually matches the lives of the people on the street, but this doesn't make the film any less disorientating to watch. There was one scene that I felt was impressive visually, and that would be the story of the apartment where we went through all the minor drug dealers that inhabited the same apartment. Not coincidentally that scene was also shot completely still, using cross-fades and overlays to construct the story rather than using multiple camera angles. Unfortunately that scene is an example of my problem with the voice over, because the story could have easily just been shown to us but rather there was a non-stop narration throughout. What the film did have working for it was a handful of decent performances. The lead, Alexandre Rodrigues as Rocket, gave a very enjoyable performance, I especially liked his character during the relationship scenes. I was very disappointed with Rodrigues's vocal performance, to be honest I found his voice very dreary and tiresome to listen to, making him the worst person to choose for the narrator, but my gripe with his voice is probably just because of how much I had to listen to it. I also liked Seu Jorge, who played Knockout Ned. Jorge should have been given a lot more time on screen. I found his character the most understanding and was extremely disappointed when his transformation into a hoodlum was brushed over in a couple of scenes. I also thought Matheus Nachtergaele, who played Carrot, was given far too little time on screen. Especially considering how big a role Carrot played in the story, I don't see why Nachtergaele wasn't given his own segment. The only gang leader that was properly represented was Li'l Zé, who happened to be my favourite character. I liked Lil' Dice's climb to the top, I really liked the child actor who played Lil' Dice, Douglas Silva, I liked his spiritual sub-plot. I liked his relationship with Benny, a character and performance (Phellipe Haagensen) that is given too much credit. I think the best thing this film does is tell the story of Li'l Zé from start to finish, and it shows that if the film wasn't so bogged down with multiple narratives and side-characters that don't amount to anything, it can actually tell a competent story. If a film ends and I don't care what happened to the protagonist, the film has failed. City of God manages to rip all of the character and humanity out of a film based around the lives of people. I wouldn't call it my favourite Paul Thomas Anderson film, but if you want to watch a movie that has as complex a conjoined narrative structure as well as a very emotional story, watch Magnolia . City of God was just obnoxious and difficult for me to watch from start to finish. That doesn't take away the good performances and occasional interesting visual, but those two things are far away from saving this film. I'm in the minority with this film and I'm sure plenty of people will strongly disagree with me, so I recommend you give it a watch yourself, but personally I didn't enjoy it and wouldn't go out of my way to watch it again.

I'm sorry to say this didn't really work for me at all. Perhaps it was my raised expectations, with this movie being prominent on both the Letterboxd and IMDb top 250 lists, as well as having received breathless comparisons to other crime dramas like Goodfellas. And I can see where the comparison comes from. City of God (Citade de Deus) has a similarly freewheeling style of editing to Thelma Schoonmaker's work, and utilises needle drops to ground everything with a temporal specificity - if nothing else, the use of "Kung Fu Fighting" is particularly choice. But whilst lofty ambitions are good, Fernando Meirelles' and Katia Lund's efforts fell short for me in several key areas. First and foremost was the style of the thing. I have to imagine the intent of the filmmakers was to set an ironic contrast between the hyper-stylised visual palette and the kitchen sink realism of the story. In practice it felt to me like asking Michael Bay to helm a remake of La Haine, neorealism by way of crass and lurid commercial and music video aesthetic. It's a visual palette that consistently seems to be screaming out "Look how awesome this is!" when the intent of the film is apparently to show just how terrible this life is and these conditions are. It's a choice that might have worked for me had the movie taken up the perspective of one of the gangsters, who would no doubt have seen their lifestyle as big and gaudy and glamourous. But our point of view is Rocket, who at all times seems pretty disgusted by what's going on around him, and seems to want little else but to get out of the favela and be a photographer. Framing his perspective with the look and feel of a Bad Boys movie felt to me like a betrayal of that perspective and of the character, and it acted as a barrier between me and the film, pushing me away rather than drawing me into the drama. My other big issue was with the way the story ended up being set out. Zipping around in time, that Scorsese influence is in evidence again as seeming scores of characters are introduced over the runtime. But due to the vignette nature of the storytelling, I found it tough to form any attachment to just about any of them. I ended up liking Benny the most, I think by virtue of his being the most likable and his motivations being the most scrutable. Even our POV character Rocket felt like a bit of a blank to me, since even though he gets the lion's share of the screen time, he's mostly used as a cypher to tell everyone else's stories. In a discussion, I've had it suggested to me that the point of building the story this way is that it is intended to be more sociological than psychological, to elicit sympathy for the overall situation in this favela than any individual characters. For me this had the opposite effect; in failing to build my empathy for any of the individuals involved, it didn't evoke my overall sympathy. Honestly I'm bummed out. I really did want to like this one but at every turn it kept failing to work for me. I'm very obviously in a minority, judging by the overall score and reception to it. I only wish I'd seen what apparently everyone else has in this thing.

City of God is a film based on the true story of life in the Brazilian slums. It has a little coming-of-age drama, and tells about some boys who grow up and take very different paths in their lives. It seems to be a real struggle for kids to lift themselves out of this difficult place to live, and to escape the dangers of the drug trade. As a result of the atmosphere in the City of God there are no perfectly pure heroes, or even perfectly evil villains. In fact, one of the most interesting aspects of this movie is the way they manipulate the audience into rooting for different people at different times. Even Lil Ze, who starts out as the clear-cut villain, actually brings peace to the slums for a time and we sympathize with him when he experiences loss. I also loved how they gave such distinct nicknames to all the characters. Where it could be easy to get lost in the sea of faces, we are easily able to tell everyone apart because they have such unique names. I did struggle to stay invested in the film, however. I wasn't finding a consistent story arc. It almost felt like a historical film or something because we are just shown events in one era, then we move on to the next without any change in our protagonist or his situation. In fact the entire theme of City of God was basically the cyclical nature of violence in the slums. So by the end the entire story starts all over again. This is one of those films that was interesting to watch, but not something I would recommend to most viewers.

The bright images and frenzied editing breathe remarkable life into a film about a perpetual cycle of death. I particularly enjoyed when soundbites played on a closing door or clanging fence, embellishing the impact of an action. This is ferocious filmmaking, a shot of caffeine injected straight into celluloid. However, the broad painting of characters and the focus on environmental details in each image lend themselves better to a mosaic film than the coming-of-age tale City of God occasionally attempts to be. This is a masterful examination of violence and its ability to prey on the infallibility of youth. When characters are used in tides of brutality, it is affecting, emotional, and horrifying. But the movie's protagonist is a cipher, devoid of any interesting traits. For a film presented with such character, Rocket has almost none. His role as an audience stand-in creates too much stability for a film that is often chaotic. Navigating this world should be a difficult process and a test of morals, but Rocket's existence lays out a clear pathway that any viewer can follow. With an obvious through line, the movie becomes a sort of tour of savagery and the impact of the tragedy is never truly felt as a result. Focusing on a central character is counter-intuitive to City of God's central conceit of painting a picture of cyclical brutality. Narrative problems aside, the exhilarating presentation of City of God is too stimulating to pass up. The vibrance of the deep oranges and blue skies beat down upon the citizens and entrap them in perpetual savagery. The most interesting character is the city of God itself (I hate saying that, but it's really true here), and all of its inhabitants add shades of color to its personality. From its very first scenes, in which our young photographer-protagonist finds himself trapped in the midst of a Mexican (ok, Brazilian) standoff between a street gang and the corrupt cops, City of God makes no bones about its debts to Scorsese and Tarantino. In fact, for much of the film, I was reminded of Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels, which brought to London much of the same snappy, experimental camerawork, “funny” gunplay, and street gangster-chic that’s on display here in Rio. But that metaphor only goes so far — this increasingly dark film ultimately feels very different than the breezy Lock Stock. In fact, while Scorsese, Tarantino, and Ritchie gangsters all generally find themselves on the wrong side of the law as a calling, the Brazilian youths here are born into it — crime, violence, and murder are an inescapable part of the Cidade de Deus. Or is it? I know this movie is based on a novel based on real events, but at a certain point, right after the strobelight-marked murder of one of the film’s most likable characters, City of God just gets lost in its own cycle of violence. When L’il Ze, the cruelest hoodlum we meet on our travels, brutally rapes the girlfriend of Knockout Ned (we never see her again — she’s a plot point, not a character), a gang war ensues that drastically escalates the already considerable levels of death and carnage the audience has to deal with. In this final third, the film derails…it’s just too much. (Ken Turan aptly summed it up as “overkill.”) One goes from avidly following the travails of individual characters to watching most or all of them go down in a hail of gunfire. Like I said, I know that much of this tale is based on a real gang war, and that the ridiculously high body count at the end of the film may have a solid grounding in fact. But at times City of God wants to have it both ways. When innocent bystanders are mowed down or child gangsters are forced to make extremely grisly life-and-death choices, we’re shocked sullen by the events depicted here. But when L’il Ze blows away his stooge Tuba in a fit of frustration, it’s a sight gag. In sum, with swooping camerawork, great performances across the board, and a well-crafted narrative, City of God bridges the gap between Tarantino-cool gangsterism and shocking acts of violence reasonably well for its first two-thirds. Alas, it falters in the final act, and I found myself spending the last thirty-five minutes of a movie I’d quite enjoyed up til then keeping my head down and waiting for the last reports of gunfire to die away. Well worth seeing if you’re a fan of the hyperkinetic gangster genre, but ultimately City of God just can’t quite close the deal. Film #26: Around the World in 30 Days (May 2014 Challenge) Country : Brazil Violence is one big, long, grueling, and—most importantly—circular chain of events. Once you pull a trigger, the bullet eventually ricochets back to you, and unless you never shoot a gun at all, there’ll be no escaping the destruction that violence leaves in its wake. Welcome, my friends, to the world of City of God , a pulsating crime drama that chronicles the rise of organized crime in the titular Brazilian favela since its inception in 1960. Told from the perspective of a young man named Rocket, we see the unrelenting cycle of gangs, guns, drugs, vendettas, victories, defeats, corpses, cops, and cash repeat itself time after time; the scenarios play out differently, but the core elements all remain the same. While there is some mild humor mixed in at times, for the most part Fernando Meirelles keeps things dark and grim, and by the end of it all the body count is so high that it would be pointless to keep track of or tally. Let’s just say that this is A Very Serious Movie, and if you’re not prepared for the level of violence it serves up, you might as well look elsewhere. What’s especially notable about the film is its emphasis on its characters, most of whom are greatly fleshed out with the help of backstories and exposition. I liked this attention to the characters because it really drove the motif of circularity home, as well as gave the amateur actors a real chance to shine as individuals. The cast list is fairly large, but that never becomes an issue due to how to the narrative weaves the disparate character threads together to form an intricately-composed whole. And without this character-driven approach, there’s no way someone like Lil Zé would have been nearly as compelling (and I think it’s pretty much agreed upon that Zé is one hell of a villain). While some films are sorely lacking in believable characters, City of God is teeming with them… and, for me, that may be its saving grace. For, you see, I did not especially enjoy City of God . I won’t deny that it’s an accomplished and no-holds-barred take on the tragic realities of slum life, but I have to admit all the same that I struggled to get through it. I wasn’t big on Meirelles’ shaky camerawork for one, and the use of voiceover for both narration and exposition was a tiresome device after a while. I’m also still trying to work out what I gleaned from the film at the end of the day; aside from its cyclical (not to mention cynical) treatment of violence and retribution, it was all so morbid that not thinking about it too much seems like the best course of action. I know Rocket’s arc ends on a hopeful note, but everything else in the film is so plagued with dire consequences and ill-fated decisions that it never registers as powerfully as it should. Sure, the film is entertaining to a point (anything that gets your adrenaline rushing is), and it’s put together with great skill and flourish, but I’m having trouble seeing why it’s so acclaimed. Am I not its intended audience, or is there something I’m missing? Maybe I’ll just wait for the day when I run into someone who worships this film and they can make their case for it. I don’t think I ever want to sit through it again, but I’m always open to hearing a well-crafted argument. Until then, I’m going to have to side-eye City of God ’s high placement on IMDb’s Top 250 list and wonder what all the fuss is about.

This Brazilian film, firmly entrenched in the coveted top-25 highest rated films on IMDB, is the true-story about two boys growing up in the violent "City Of God" neighborhood outside of Rio De Janiero in Brazil - one becomes a photographer, the other a murderous drug-dealer. The 130-minute story feels like a Portuguese version of Scorsese's "Goodefllas" - except with delusional and hopeless children, rather than Ray Liotta and Robert DeNiro. Perhaps it was because of the subtitles, or because all the children looked so similar, or perhaps it was the non-linear and sporadic narrative, but I found myself struggling to follow the complicated plot and character paths for most of the first half of this film. When things finally settled in, and after most of the supporting cast had been killed off - I was pleasantly surprised by "City Of God" - which finally started to come into its own, rather than a string of familiar scenes of people getting murdered. The immensely large cast of local amateurs all did a terrific job, but none of them really stood-out, and I found it difficult to really connect to any of the main characters. I will say this though: the cinematography and editing in this film were absolutely outstanding - keeping things moving at a blistering pace, all while maintaining a very stylized, almost music-video look to some of the shots. The dirty slums of Rio are portrayed with gritty and striking realism that really immerses you in the sounds and sights of this hellish neighborhood. And although this film, and all of its characters are closely based on a true-story, I couldn't help but feel like it was poor-man's version of much better gangster films that had come before. Although beautifully shot, written, and acted - I quite honestly wasn't that impressed with "City Of God", I'd go so far as to say I was even bored at times. Going in with high expectations was probably a mistake, but I really didn't think this movie was anything special. That being said however, I did enjoy the film, especially the last hour - and I can certainly appreciate it for what it was trying to accomplish - so it wins back some points from me there. There were aspects I thoroughly enjoyed, and thought were quite deserving of a higher ratings, while at other times, I found myself disconnected and uninterested with the plot... I thought it was GOOD.

After years of people telling me this film was good I finally sat down two nights ago to watch it. I was furious. Furious that it had taken me this long to see it. It was nothing like I had expected. It was warm and funny and terrifyingly violent. It made you feel like you could empathise with the main character despite the fact that no one I know lives in conditions or circumstances like this. It was that rarest of film. One that is a universal story set in a world that couldn’t be more specific. My favourite character was the tragi-hero Knockout Ned. It wasn’t until the movie finished that I realised where I knew him from. He was the wicked Brazilian guitar player, Pele dos Santos from “The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou”. The vibrant cuts and hyper realistic violence felt like a mixing pot between Scorcese, Tarantino, Aronofsky and Ritchie but never actually felt like it was ripping off any of them but rather developing it’s own style. The scene where Cabeleria is running away from the police after trying to push start the car was one of the most beautiful things I have ever seen. Buscapé: It was like a message from God: “Honesty doesn’t pay, sucker.”

It is a chilling, but very human, depiction of the vicious cycle formed by corruption and poverty in the Third World.

‘Cidade de Deus’ (City of God) is a Brazilian crime drama chronicling the lives of a group of Brazilian street kids & the growth of organised crime in a suburb of Rio de Janeiro. The film itself is brutal and has a frightening realism that you can only find by casting locals who have lived this life, there is little wonder that these youngsters descend into this life as they are pretty much damned either way. Only one of the boys ‘Rocket’ has no desire to be a criminal, he likes hanging out with his friends & develops a keen interest in photography, but staying out of the circle & staying alive are not certainties, even if you decide to live within the law. Driven by the local and completely unknown cast, this film is breathtaking from start to finish, brilliantly acted, beautifully shot and more than deserving of the plaudits directed towards it at the time of its international release. Which only makes be wish that I’d seen it earlier. Highly recommended viewing.

City of God is more than just a detailed look at life in the slums, and more than a fierce play on the Gangster genre. It's a morality plague for the mind, but only in the best way. If you don't get sucked up in the story  then there's plenty for your thoughts to chew on here. But what truly gives it that place in our minds as one of the greatest pieces of modern cinema is the way in which the two genres compliment each other. It doesn't set out to be shocking and nor does it try to set up many obvious connections to the gangster genre. Even when it isn't subtle, it's inventive and when it's subtle it opens out to be stimulative and embracing. But its ambition for being truly realistic allows it to leave an impression much grander than any scene purely designed for shock value ever could.

To sum it up: a masterpiece. One of the finest films of the 2000s and of all time for that matter. And I can definitely understand why it has been compared to Goodfellas . Apart from sharing detailed storylines that dig deep into the criminal underworld & an expert narration [and some seriously funny dialogue], both boast of stellar filmmaking craftsmanship; especially with the editing and, of course, the directing. Like Scorsese's masterpiece, there is a rhythmic flow involved here... it's infused with a kinetic sort of energy in the non-linear storytelling... it starts at full throttle and never slows down. Stunning cinematography/colour compositions and terrific use of music as well. And the performances? Simply amazing, especially when you take into account most of the cast were nonprofessional actors - in particular, the actors who play the Li'l Zé character together create one of the best villains in celluloid history. An outstanding film in every aspect; horrifying with its realism, funny through its characters and riveting as an experience. I implore to you: just see it once; you'll find it difficult to erase it from your mind.

I love City of God but its been many years since I saw it. Going back to 2006 probably. Its the film that opened up Brazil for me. I've seen many great Brazilian films since this one. The favelas give Brazilian cinema a hard edge. The inner city crime of major American cities intensified by their third world poverty. City of God is a multi-layered character study, which gave it the reputation of "Brazilian Goodfellas" for quite some time. But City of God deserves to be paid attention to for all its own merits. The first 30 minutes are absolutely stunning and are basically an epilogue. Those opening 30 minutes are better than most entire films. If you've never seen this, you need to include it your December Project lists.

Approximately seven years ago I had the opportunity to watch Fernando Meirelles’ and Kátia Lund’s City of God, but through a combination of naivety, stupidity and a ridiculous abstention from subtitled films I allowed it, along with many other foreign language films, to completely pass me by. As the film begins, with its stunning opening sequence of sensational stylistics, jarring jump cuts and snaring sound editing – an evocative introduction to the compelling, yet devastating film we’re about to witness – I am reminded of a period where I shamefully ignored a truly remarkably proportion of cinema. City of God is an unflinching presentation of gang life within Rio de Janeiro and depicts the development of a violent criminal underworld within the socially, economically and racially isolated favela. It’s a captivating piece of cinema, gloriously captured and exceptionally performed. To this day there are plenty of people who remain as close-minded as I previously was and that’s the biggest shame. Essentially, all I’m trying to say is that this masterpiece is not a rarity for world cinema and removing yourself from it is a massive mistake.
